I’ve run out of chucks. Well, not really, but I may have to set aside my current must-try project and commit to completing my other projects that are still sitting in chucks awaiting some
off-lathe embellishment or finishing prior to finishing them off on the lathe. Novel concept
that – resisting new projects and focussing on completing all my works in progress. Think
of the satisfaction I would get when all my turning projects are completed! Think of all the
new projects I can start and set aside for the next cycle.
Then again, I could resort to swapping jaws on one of my few remaining chucks and ignoring
for now the incomplete works-in-progress. But that is not something I really relish doing.
The jaws on those chucks were probably installed years before I started putting anti-seize
lubricant on the jaw screws. I can already see the drills, screw extractors and colourful language being unleashed. (sigh). I know I’ll have to bite the bullet one day, but does it really
have to be today?
Alternatively, I could be lazy, avoid the inevitable frustration and just finish off the project
that’s sitting in the chuck I want to use. Or I could be even lazier, with a bit of sadness, take
a good, hard look at each WIP and decide to vote one of them off the bench and into the
firewood bin. I guess it all comes down to how lazy will I have to admit to being? Something
I will have to ponder before heading back out to my workshop. Who would have thought that
woodturning could be so brutally introspective?
At the beginning of last summer, it became apparent that pandemic lockdowns and restrictions would be with us for many months to come. At that time, I, along with most board
members, had grave concerns about how the club would look after September/October as
memberships all came up for renewal during the pandemic. We heard that other clubs were
seeing renewal rates below 50% and discovered some other clubs who seemed to have
ceased operation altogether.
The executive and a few volunteers spent a great deal of time discussing, planning, and implementing initiatives we hoped would reunite members who got “lost” in our sudden shift to
online meetings, keep our membership engaged and provide great value for your membership dues during these difficult times. We were encouraged with the rising attendance at our
monthly online meetings and Thursday evening chats and had received a few very positive
and encouraging emails from members.
Nevertheless, we were braced for a worse case scenario. As eTransfers and cheques began to trickle in at the middle of September I began bugging our Treasurer every few days
for membership numbers. The numbers began to pickup near the end of September into
October and by the end of October I began to let out a sigh of relief.
I am absolutely over the moon to be able to report that, as I am writing this less than a week

before our November meeting, we have 96 members! I would like to express by deepest
thank you to everyone who has worked so hard over the past several months to make this
happen. I especially want to thank all our members who have renewed their memberships
and the several new members who have joined our group over the past few months for
supporting our guild. I am so grateful for everyone’s participation and enthusiasm.
Our Annual General Meeting will take place online at 6:30pm sharp on February 25th just
before our guest presenter. We will be electing a new Treasurer along with a couple
Members at Large. If you are interested in getting more involved with the leadership of
the GVWG you are encouraged to consider standing for an open board position.
We have Dustin Cook to thank for organizing an amazing lineup of speakers for the next
several months starting with our own Larry Stevenson who will be demonstrating our November monthly meeting. Phil Irons from the UK will be providing us with a Saturday
morning demo on how to turn a “caddy spoon” on December 5th. We kick the new year off
at our January meeting with a presentation on everything you ever wanted to know about
spalted wood by Dr. Seri Robinson. February’s meeting features John Beaver from California. Eric Lofstrom from Washington state will be presenting at our March meeting.
April brings us another Saturday morning demonstration by Richard Findlay from the UK.
Greg Gallegos from Michigan will demonstrating at our May meeting. You can see more
information these events on our website.
Stay safe!
Steve

YOUR Website Gallery Banner
As you know, Bruce Campbell has resigned as editor of our newsletter after holding that
position for over 6 years during which we have had the best or one of the best newsletters
in the AAW. As In many other guild positions held by Bruce, he has provided us with extraordinary level of effort, insight and dedication from which we all have benefitted. I have
agreed to be the new editor and can only hope to keep up to Bruce’s high standards.
As a longtime member of the guild, I have found that I know many, but not all, of the other
members. However, I often do not know as much about their turning skills and interests as
I would like to know while of others I know very little except to recognize them at our
monthly meetings. I expect this is true for many of you; something exacerbated by our inability to meet in person during this pandemic. So, I think one remedy would be to introduce
a new column in the newsletter in which we can profile one of our members and their work.
As you will see below, we will start this ball rolling with Georges Bois, our newest member
who has just joined us this month.
If you have any additional ideas for columns or changes to the newsletter that you would
like to see, please contact me at editor@gvwg.ca
Des Wilson Steve Fairbairn

Trent Bosch—Vessel of Illusion
We were fortunate to have Trent Bosch as our main speaker last month and, of course, it
was over ZOOM. Trent has been here before and given this very demonstration in person as part of a day-long demo. Yet this was hardly repetitive. Trent has, as usual,
gone to great care in his ZOOM setup to the point that his camera placements and
smooth presentation made us feel like we were right there. He also allowed for real-time
questions which increased the sense that we were right there. My intention was to write
a detailed report of the demo but in searching the web for a copy of his initial “steps of
hollowing” diagram I came across an excellent write-up done by the Carolina Mountain
Woodturners Guild. Never one to re-invent the wheel if I don’t have to, I invite you to visit their excellent site at:
https://carolinamountainwoodturners.org/demonstrations/trent-bosch-demonstrates-forcmw-on-august-17-2019/
Thanks Trent for a great demo and thanks as well to CMW for the great report.

Tech Talk continues to be held at 7:00 PM
on the Monday evening following our Guild
Zoom meeting. We will stay with this arrangement as long as we are ZOOM-ing
rather than meeting at Sapperton Hall. As
usual, a link to the session will be emailed
to all paid-up members. Please join in and
bring along your question and share you
experiences.
Chris started us off with a follow-up to his
project from last time – turning a full-sized
rugby ball. Last time he was looking for
suggestions to transfer images to the surface. This time he was asking about texturing the surface to give it that dimpled leather look.
•
Larry suggested the basic approach
would be a ball bur in a rotary tool.
While this would not be fast it is probably the most controllable solution
•
Several of us suggested a modified
welder’s needle scalar. The modification is to round the ends of each rod in
the scaler so they dent the surface of
the wood rather than crack it. When using the tool it is best to go for gentle
pressure at first until you can gauge the
impact
Chris then wondered if texturing it first
would complicate transferring the images.
We all agreed it certainly would so best to
apply the images first and then texture
around them afterwards.
Steve F was up next with a diagnosis of
why his hollowing project failed. He decided it was mostly because he was using the
wrong tool. He was using a gooseneck bar
while trying to widen the initial drilled hole.
The back edge of the gooseneck fouled on
the back side of the hole, lifted the bar off
the toolrest and “rigorously” moved it to the
left. In the process the lip of the opening
got broken. He was using the gooseneck
because that was all he had which lead to
the “obvious” solution; Steve has since purchased a straight bar and a slightly offset
one as well.
Meanwhile, Steve was also been building a
visualizer system that allows the user to
track where the cutter is when inside a hollow form. He purchased an inexpensive
camera and monitor along with some adapter cables and should soon be able to tackle
much more complicated vessels. There are
a number of articles and videos on visualizer systems. If you are interested I recommend you have a look. I particularly like
this one that uses a backup camera with a
7” monitor included:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?
v=UpHdjFFs1bc
Gary gave us some follow-up information
on his problem from last time of oil not drying. We had suggested that he could use
polymerized tung oil over top. He tried that
and reported that it did indeed dry and provide him with a better finish.
Gary still prefers a glossier finish because
they sell better in his market of craft fairs
and farmers market. Yet, the time needed
to build up a high gloss using Wipe-on-Poly
is a barrier for him. He has been playing
with different finishes and reports that he
does not like OBIE Juice but is trying a reci-
(Continued on page 7)

pe of 40% Tung oil, 50% Spar Varnish; and
10 Paint Thinner. He will report back with
results. Steve warned that Spar Varnish is
designed to remain pliable after it dries and
may present issues on bowl. We look forward to the results of Gary’s tests.
Gary went on to talk about the Sorby Texturing System. This is a popular tool but Gary
reports that it is not easy to use. It takes
some time to master the angles, pressures,
and changes in grain orientation. However,
once you “get it” it is a great tool for adding
decorative details to a piece.
Steve H. made a hollowing bar with an articulating head.
It’s a 1 ½ inch arm that is attached to a ½
inch shank. The arm is locked in place with a
small screw, tapped into the shank and has a
90 degree swing. He uses a 3/16 inch bit that
is CA glued into the arm. The tools used to
make this were a drill press (cheap one),
small files, bench grinder, and tap. To
sharpen bits that are glued in place, a coarse
diamond hone is affixed to a small plastic jig
that keeps the hone level to the top of the bit.
A few strokes and it is sharpened. This method is quick, repeatable, and it maintains the
cutter bit’s profile.
We saw Trent Bosch demonstrate his carving vice that fits in the lathe banjo (see photo)
And Steve H. showed his version of the rig.
He uses the tail vice on his work bench to
hold the post for his version of a carving
stand.

Finally, I reported that I was given a rare timber to try. A family friend took down a Persian Ironwood tree (Parrotia Presica) and I
got several nice pieces including 2 crotches.
I can report that it is dense, has solid forks
(no bark inclusions) with thin feathers, is a
light creamy yellowish-white colour, and
turns beautifully. I microwaved a 14” x 8”
bowl that dried with little warping and sanded
well afterwards. Two downsides to this
wood; it is rare and the chips smells like a
cow pasture after a heavy rain. But, on balance, I am looking forward to making more
pieces with it.
Please attend our next session by joining our
ZOOM call at 7:00 on Monday November
30th. As usual, the ZOOM details will be
emailed to all paid-up members a few days
before the meeting. I look forward to seeing
you there.

The piece is called the Watchman.
Not every day you get a slab of maple burl like this
so I really thought hard to what to apply to it.
Turning this slab was a lot of fun. Using vacuum
chucks to hold the wood while turning my tenon
made it a lot easier.
The dimensions are 22" tall by 17" wide. Thickness
is 1/2" on the outside and just under 2" in the middle.
My biggest challenge was the ghost shadow it does
smart when it gets you.
Trying to make small details without making it to
busy and not using a lot of colour to over power it.

I was asked to write a brief description of
how I do fused glass and combine it with
woodturning. The photos show various
ways that I Have used glass combined with
wood.
The first thing to do is to plan the piece, because it is much easier to shape the wood
than the glass. Make your glass piece first,
then fit the wood to it. It is easier with both
media to subtract material than to add to it!
Fused glass is glass cut into shapes, then
fired in a kiln. Various coloured glasses are
available but one should use glass designed for fusing. Heated glass wants to be
6mm (1/4”) thick and will expand or contract
to reach that thickness, which can affect
your
shapes.
Differently
manufactured
glasses have different coefficients of expansion (COE) and cannot be mixed in a fused
piece. I use Bullseye Glass, with a COE of
90, but Spectrum Glass, with a COE of 96
is more readily available to purchase here.
If you mix them your product is guaranteed
to crack!
The kiln I have is a Paragon kiln designed
for fusing glass. It was the largest kiln available at the time that used 120V electricity.
That was about 14 years ago. There are
different ones now. My kiln will do a 10”
square or several smaller pieces at a time.
It can also be programmed for slumping or
fire-polishing. The other tools are primarily
for glass cutting and are the same as those
used for stained glass work.
To shape the flat fused discs into bowls or
lids for boxes the pieces are placed in or on
molds. Ceramic molds are used to slump
into, e.g., for bowls, and stainless steel
molds are used to slump over, e.g., as lids
for boxes. Then they are ready for use.
I find that using glass is an interesting way
to bring colour to my turnings without applying colour to the wood. As you can see from
the photos, you can add or include the
glass in a variety of boxes and platters.
Good Luck if you try this!
Trudy

Guild Member Profile - Georges Bois
1. Tell us about your background – how
did you get into woodturning?
My father loved woodturning. He started
turning with a drill that he made into a small
lathe. Then he bought a small lathe on
which I started. I was hooked!
2. Tell us about your workshop/ studio.
It’s a constant work in progress.
3. What tools do you most like using on
your lathe?
Any tool, really ! As long as it’s sharp. I love
the bowl gouge.
4. What is your favourite wood.
Box wood, Yew, olive. I’m discovering the
woods from BC.
5. What finishes do you prefer using?
Either nothing or beeswax mix
6. Do you ever incorporate other materials
into your pieces?
Occasionally gold or silver leaves. But usually not. I like plain wood.
(Continued on page 13)
Olive Wood Crotch

Page 13
GVWG
7. What other types of woodworking or
pursuits do you have?
Collecting any piece of wood with an interesting shape. Drift wood or else.
8. What inspires you – where do you get
your ideas from?
From the piece of wood itself. It’s the
beauty in the wood that calls to be revealed.
9. Who has been the greatest influence
on your work?
My Dad was the first one. Then it was
self exploration.
10. Where do you usually display and/or
sell your work?
At home!
11. What is the most challenging piece
that you have made so far?
See the photo of a walnut slab I kept
square on my small lathe.
12. Where do you see your work going in
the future?
I’d love to update my self-taught techniques to a safer, more efficient level.
Like go back to basics.
13. Are there any new techniques you
would like to try?
Epoxy. Hollowing of a vase. Boxes
14. Where do you think you most need to
improve?
Sharpening my tools!

➢ Always wear safety goggles or safety glasses that
include side protectors. Use a full face shield for
bowl, vessel, or any turning involving chucks and
faceplates.
➢ Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder
and wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
➢ Wear hearing protection during extended periods
of turning.
➢ Turn the lathe off before adjusting the tool rest or
tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
➢ Always remove chuck keys, adjusting wrenches,
and knockout bars immediately after use. Never
leave them in place, even for a moment.
➢ Tie back long hair and avoid loose clothing, jewelry,
or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating
parts or accessories.
➢ When using a faceplate, be certain the workpiece is
solidly mounted with stout screws (#10 or #12
sheet metal screws as a minimum). Do not use dry
wall or deck screws.
➢ When turning between centers, be certain the
workpiece is firmly mounted between the headstock driving center and tailstock center.
➢ Ensure the belt guard or cover is in place.
➢ Check that all locking devices on the tailstock and
tool rest assembly (rest and base) are tight before
operating the lathe.
➢ Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
➢ Rotate your workpiece backwards by hand to make
sure it clears the toolrest and bed before turning
the lathe on.
➢ Stay clear of the areas directly behind and in front
of the workpiece, they are the most likely areas for
a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good
safety habit is to step out of this zone when turning
on the lathe, keeping your hand on the switch in
case you need to turn the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
➢ Always check the speed of the lathe before turning
it on. Use slower speeds for larger diameters or
rough pieces and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a
piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always stop the
machine to verify why. As a starting point, consult
your operator’s manual for recommended speeds
for a particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed is
compatible with the size of the blank.
➢ Exercise extra caution when using stock with
cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets, knots, irregular
shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid
these types of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
➢ Hold turning tools securely on the toolrest, holding
the tool in a controlled but comfortable manner.
Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
➢ Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is
possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless
it is securely tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
You mostly turn alone so safety is YOUR responsibility.
Safety Guidelines for Wood Turning

Page 17
GVWG
You mostly turn alone so safety is YOUR responsibility.
Safety Guidelines for Wood Turning
➢ Know your capabilities and limitations. An experienced woodturner is capable of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning turners.
➢ Always remove the tool rest before sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
➢ Don’t overreach, keep proper footing, and keep
your balance at all times.
➢ Keep your lathe in good repair. Check for damaged parts, alignment, binding of moving parts,
and other conditions that may affect its operation.
➢ Keep tools sharp and clean for better and safer
performance. Don’t force a dull tool. Don’t use a
tool for a purpose for which it was not designed or
intended.
➢ Consider your work environment. Don’t use a
lathe in damp or wet locations. Do not use in presence of inflammable liquids or gases, and always
keep a fully-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
➢ Stay alert. Watch what you are doing. Pay close
attention to unusual sounds or vibrations. Stop
the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate
machines when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
➢ Guard against electric shock. Inspect electric
cords for damage. Avoid the use of extension
cords.
➢ Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn
power off. Don’t leave lathe until it comes to a
complete stop.
➢ Many accidents to woodturners occur while using
saws, especially band and chain saws. Learn and
follow the safety guidelines for this equipment.

Saturday December 5 at 11:00am
Phil Irons Demonstration
Join us for a special Saturday morning interactive remote demonstration by Phil Irons from the UK on Saturday, December 5th at 11:00am PST. Phil will be
demonstrating how to turn Caddy Spoons.
Phil is the current President of the Association of
Woodturners of Great Britain, a member of the American Association of Woodturners and a Registered
Professional Turner.
He has won numerous awards in national competitions and is regularly invited to teach and demonstrate his techniques nationally and at an international
level, including, France, Belgium, Spain, Germany,
Finland, Ireland, Italy, Norway, South Africa, New
Zealand and the USA. Phil is the author of several
magazine articles and a best selling project book
“Woodturning, Two in One” that has been translated
into nine languages.
He is best known for his coloured vessels and hollow forms with their clear, beautiful
shapes and flowing lines, always striving for the perfect form. He uses wood salvaged
from tree surgeons and firewood merchants. This wood often has no other commercial
value other than as firewood.
